title: Carrying the sutra (section 15)
hook: one who keeps and explains this sutra carries awakening on their shoulders

segments.voice: Yesterday, Subhuti wept. He heard the teaching on no fixed self, and the tears came, and the Buddha remembered being cut apart by a king without anger. Your line: he wept to hear it. Did anything you heard yesterday move you? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-two.

A backpack strap digs into one shoulder. A toddler rides on a parent's shoulders at a parade, gripping two fistfuls of hair. A friend says, I've got this one, and takes the heavier box up the stairs. Shoulders are where we put the things that matter enough to haul. Section fifteen of the Diamond Sutra reaches for that same part of the body. After all its talk of giving and merit, the Buddha says something about the people who keep this teaching: they carry awakening on their shoulders. Today: carrying the sutra.
screen: `A STRAP, A CHILD, A BOX.` → `SHOULDERS HAUL WHAT MATTERS.` → `SECTION FIFTEEN.`

segments.voice: First, the scale. The section opens with a picture too big to hold. Someone gives up their own body, the sutra says, as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, in the morning, again at noon, again in the evening, age after age. And the Buddha says that someone who simply hears this teaching and trusts it, without turning against it, has more merit than that. Second, the ladder. Hearing and trusting is the first rung. Then come those who copy it out, keep it, recite it, and explain it to others. Each step moves the teaching along: from the ear, to the hand, to the mouth, to another person. Keeping, here, isn't storing a book on a shelf. It's holding the words close enough that they get used. The Buddha says this sutra is spoken for those who have set out on the great vehicle, the path of awakening for the sake of everyone. Third, the shoulders. The Tathagata knows such people, the sutra says, and sees them, and they carry the Tathagata's awakening on their shoulders. Awakening, in that picture, isn't a private prize. It's a weight that gets passed along, the way a family carries a recipe or a trade. The sutra adds a warning, in the sharp language of an old argument between schools: those who delight in lesser teachings, and cling to the idea of a self, can't really hear this one. That's the sutra's claim, not a verdict on anyone. Fourth, the paradox. This is the same sutra that keeps saying there is no fixed self, no merit to hold onto, nothing to grasp. And now it asks to be carried. Some readers find the point right there. You can carry something without owning it. A parent carries a sleeping child home from the car and never once thinks, this child is my possession. The weight is real. The grip is light.
screen: `GIVING SANDS OF BODIES.` · `HEAR, COPY, KEEP, RECITE, EXPLAIN.` · `AWAKENING ON THE SHOULDERS.` · `CARRIED, NOT OWNED.` · then, large: `ON YOUR SHOULDERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: carry one teaching today. Settle, and let your breath slow. Notice your shoulders. Let them drop a little, away from your ears. Now pick up one line from the last few days of this sutra: a mind that rests on nothing, perhaps, or beyond the marks. Let it settle across the shoulders, like a strap you've adjusted to fit. Then walk through the rest of today in your mind: the commute, the dishes, the hard phone call. At each stop, ask what the line would change there. Rest with the breath and the weight together, firm and light at once. The bell holds the time.
Carrying the sutra. In section fifteen, those who keep, recite and explain this teaching carry the Tathagata's awakening on their shoulders. Today's word.

Your line: on your shoulders. Today, when you pick up a bag, a box or a child, let the weight remind you of the line you're carrying, and pass it to one person. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: In some Mahayana communities the Diamond Sutra is copied by hand, recited aloud, and taught to others, which the sutra itself names as ways of keeping it.

original.note: Sanskrit for a teaching text like this one; the Pali form is sutta.

trapdoor: what you thought: carrying the sutra means owning a copy.
what it means: hearing, copying, keeping, reciting and explaining it, and so carrying awakening on your shoulders.
what a scholar hears: a sutra that denies any fixed self still asks to be carried; the burden is real, the grip is not.

notes: Section 15 paraphrased, not quoted (Max Müller's wording unverified): check the morning/noon/evening giving of bodies as many as the Ganges sands, the ladder (hear and trust, copy, keep, recite, explain), 'carry the Tathagata's awakening on their shoulders', and the warning about those attached to small teachings and the idea of a self.
'The great vehicle, the path of awakening for the sake of everyone' is a plain gloss of Mahayana; confirm it is fair.
Section numbering follows the traditional 32-section division used in earlier days of this block.

Editor pass: the 'small teachings' warning is now framed as the sutra's claim from an old argument between schools, not a verdict on any listener; the practice no longer repeats day 1125's recall-a-helpful-line-and-share-it, and asks the listener to carry a line from this sutra through the day instead.
